lesson.title: Direction Matters: Understanding Vectors
lesson.summary: A vector carries both a magnitude and a direction, and operations like addition, scalar multiplication, and the dot product let you combine vectors and measure the angle between them.
lesson.body:
A vector is a quantity that has both size (magnitude) and direction, unlike a scalar, which is just a single number. Velocity is a good everyday example: saying a car travels at 60 miles per hour is a scalar description of speed, but saying it travels 60 miles per hour due north is a vector description, because direction is now part of the information. On the coordinate plane, a vector is often written as an ordered pair like v = (3, 4), understood as an arrow starting at the origin and ending at the point (3, 4), though vectors can be positioned anywhere as long as their length and direction are preserved.

The magnitude of a vector (x, y) is found with the same idea as the distance formula, since the vector's components form the legs of a right triangle and the vector itself is the hypotenuse: |v| = √(x² + y²). For v = (3, 4), the magnitude is √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. Adding two vectors is done component by component: (3, 4) + (-1, 2) = (2, 6). Multiplying a vector by a scalar stretches or shrinks it while keeping its direction (or reversing it, if the scalar is negative): 3(3, 4) = (9, 12).

The dot product combines two vectors into a single scalar number, and it is defined as u · v = u₁v₁ + u₂v₂, multiplying corresponding components and adding the results. The dot product is especially useful because it connects directly to the angle between two vectors through the formula cosθ = (u · v)/(|u||v|). When the dot product is zero, the vectors are perpendicular, since cosθ = 0 only when θ = 90 degrees.

Here is a fully worked example using u = (3, 4) and v = (-1, 2). The dot product is u · v = (3)(-1) + (4)(2) = -3 + 8 = 5. The magnitude of u is |u| = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5, and the magnitude of v is |v| = √((-1)² + 2²) = √(1 + 4) = √5, about 2.236. Plugging into the angle formula gives cosθ = 5/(5 × √5) = 5/(5√5) = 1/√5, which is about 0.4472. Taking the inverse cosine of 0.4472 gives θ ≈ 63.4 degrees. So these two vectors point in directions that differ by roughly 63.4 degrees, information that a plain magnitude comparison could never reveal, which is exactly why direction is treated as a first-class part of the quantity rather than an afterthought.
